📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aave DAO service provider TokenLogic has proposed on Nov. 20 raising the USDC stake target for Umbrella, the protocol’s bad-debt backstop on Ethereum, from 38.84 million to 45.8 million USDC.

The proposal would also cut the extra reward APY at that target from 3.14% to 2.5%.

Recent findings suggest that if holders withdrew from the Nov. 17 cooldown queue at the historical rate with no other changes to stake, about 46 million USDC would remain staked, roughly 240,000 USDC above the proposed target. Under the same test, USDT would fall short.

The proposal would extend Umbrella rewards for USDC, USDT and WETH past their Dec. 2 expiry through April 2, 2027. TokenLogic intends to gather forum feedback before advancing the renewal to a formal Aave Improvement Proposal.

Aave’s ten latest governance proposals showed no corresponding vote or execution as of Nov. 23.

Recent findings suggest that umbrella stakers put their interest-bearing Aave deposits at risk to cover bad debt. To leave, they first start a 20-day cooldown, then have two days to withdraw.

Industry observers note that across cooldown windows closed through Oct. 26, TokenLogic found that holders withdrew 44% of the USDC and 55% of the USDT they had queued.

In a recent development, on Nov. 17, Holders had staked 53.75 million USDC, with 32.6% in cooldown. At that balance, withdrawals of about 45% from the queue would bring USDC stake down to the proposed target, only slightly above the 44% historically withdrawn.

The USDT vault held nearly 59 million staked, with 55.4% queued. Applying its historical exit share leaves about 41 million USDT, or 91% of its proposed 45.2 million target.

At historical withdrawal rates, the Nov. 17 model leaves USDC 240,000 above target and USDT nearly 4.2 million below.

Source: TokenLogic’s Nov. 20 proposal · Aave governance proposal 507.

In a recent development, on Nov. 23, CryptoKeyhole valued the USDC and USDT stakes at about $51.3 million and $46.8 million, respectively, using readings from the Ethereum contracts. Its dashboard reported stake totals without cooldown balances, so withdrawal estimates are tied to Nov. 17.

Sources indicate that active USDC loans on Aave V3 Ethereum Core rose about 36%, from $1.9 billion on June 3 to $2.6 billion on Nov. 17, according to TokenLogic. USDe and sUSDe together rose from 4% to 12% of the collateral backing those loans.

Meanwhile, the share of collateral in the group of highly liquid assets TokenLogic tracks fell from 88.5% to 77.6%.

Sources indicate that against that November loan book, the existing target amounts to 1.5% of USDC borrowing. The proposal would lift that share to 1.77%, below the roughly 2% used in June. TokenLogic also proposed cutting USDT’s extra APY at target from 3.17% to 2.5%.

Sources indicate that the 2.50% applies to the additional Umbrella reward at the target stake level. At the higher stake recorded on Nov. 17, the proposed rules would pay about 1.76% in annualized extra rewards.

TokenLogic put the total annualized yield, including deposit interest, at 7% on average over the seven days through Nov. 17.

The Aave DAO takes the first loss up to 1.3 million USDC. Beyond that offset, Umbrella can slash the USDC stake designated for the same Ethereum Core reserve and send the slashed assets to the Aave Collector to cover the deficit.

The Aave DAO’s first-loss offset sits ahead of the matching Umbrella vault on Ethereum Core.

Umbrella vaults absorb deficits in their own reserve.

The sequence shows which funds can cover an Ethereum Core USDC deficit.

Recent findings suggest that the offset comes from TokenLogic’s November proposal and Aave’s earlier governance record. The sequence follows Aave’s Umbrella contract documentation.

The sequence shows which funds can cover an Ethereum Core USDC deficit.

The loss-absorbing buffer comes from what holders stake, and ordinary Aave suppliers draw withdrawals from the lending reserve’s available USDC.

If the renewal takes effect, lending yields and the share of queued stake that leaves will help determine whether Umbrella can sustain the bigger buffer at the lower reward setting.

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If we told you tennis has been shown to boost heart health, balance, strength, mental acuity, and mood plus add nearly 10 years to your life, you might think we also had a bridge to sell you.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Tennis is a whole-body sport,” says sports medicine surgeon Alexis Colvin, MD, chief medical officer of the US Open.
  • You also don’t have to be a star tennis player to reap the longevity benefits, Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If we told you tennis has been shown to boost heart health, balance, strength, mental acuity, and mood plus add nearly 10 years to your life, you might think we also had a bridge to sell you. But it’s true: Research demonstrates that even recreational tennis can have a seriously impressive impact on your health—now and for years to come.

Recent findings suggest that “Tennis is a whole-body sport,” says sports medicine surgeon Alexis Colvin, MD, chief medical officer of the US Open. “It offers cardiovascular benefits, muscle strengthening, flexibility—all the things you need to deal with any physical challenges later in life.”.

You also don’t have to be a star tennis player to reap the longevity benefits, Dr. Colvin adds. In a 2020 study she co-authored, researchers surveyed over 10,000 tennis players, most of them recreational; about 70 percent played just one to three days a week. The players scored higher than the general population on measures such as physical strength, mental and emotional health, and social engagement. “You don't have to be playing at a very high level to get those benefits,” Dr. Colvin notes.

And those benefits appear to extend one’s life: When researchers followed 8,577 people for up to 25 years, they found that those who played tennis an average of 103 minutes a week lived 9.7 years longer than their sedentary counterparts. They also lived significantly longer than cyclists (who get an extra 3.7 years), swimmers (3.4 years), and joggers (3.2 years).

Even if you’ve never played tennis before, it’s never too late to start. Keep reading for five reasons to pick up a racket, hit the court, and do your future self a favor.

Industry observers note that tennis involves bursts of high intensity movement—sprinting to the net, running backwards to lob a volley, stopping and then lunging to the opposite side of the court to hit the ball—all of which can do wonders for your cardiovascular health. It boosts heart rate, maximizes your body’s use of oxygen, strengthens heart muscle, improves circulation, and can lower blood pressure and cholesterol levels. As a result, women who play tennis an average two to three hours a week have a 44 percent lower risk of developing cardiovascular disease and a 66 percent lower chance of dying from it.

In a recent development, when you sprint across the court, swing a racquet, or come to a sudden stop, you’re working your leg muscles, core, shoulders, back, and arms—in other words, strengthening nearly every part of the body. A recent study of more than 5,000 women between the ages 63 and 99 found that those who had greater muscle strength lived the longest. And because you’re also supporting your own body weight as you run and land, the sport also helps increase bone density, Dr. Colvin says. Stronger bones mean a lower risk of fractures and osteoporosis in the future, which is what you need if you want to age well.

Tennis requires coordinated movement and muscle control to maintain fluid footwork and smooth, continuous swings. Your core helps make that possible and is key to good balance. Both core strength and balance can help you avoid falls and fractures as you get older. Another part of balance is visuospatial skill—the ability to recognize environmental cues that help you stay upright. Tennis may help sharpen that, too. In a 2022 study, older tennis players who faced a disruption that could throw them off balance were able to react and steady themselves as well as younger players.

Industry observers note that tennis demands intense focus and decision making. “There’s a lot of active thinking going on,” Dr. Colvin says. “You’re making a lot of split-second decisions while you’re playing, plus thinking about the overall strategy of the game. That kind of mental engagement is notable as we get older.” According to research, engaging in that kind of quick and strategic thinking while being physically active may be particularly good at promoting neuroplasticity and boosting cognitive function—both of which can stave off the cognitive decline that can come with age.

Sources indicate that studies have found that people who play tennis regularly tend to be less stressed or anxious than people who do lower-intensity exercise. They also report feeling more optimistic, less depressed, and a greater sense of well-being. Like other high-energy sports, tennis may boost mood by prompting the release of brain chemicals such as endorphins, dopamine, and serotonin. It’s also a fun game to play with friends. “The social aspect of tennis is one of its key benefits,” Dr. Colvin says. Numerous studies show that those kinds of community ties are essential for a long, healthy, happier life. With tennis, that’s built into the game.

Zendaya and Tom Holland may have tied the knot, but they’re still marking upcoming milestones together. The actors have reportedly purchased their first piece of real estate together. The Daily Mail broke the news, alleging that the Spider-Man co-stars paid about $10.8 million (£8.25 million) cash for a five-bedroom house in an undisclosed London suburb described as “exclusive” and “leafy.”.

According to recent reports, there are few publicly known facts about the property—which isn’t much of a surprise, considering it took months for the notably private couple to confirm that they had gotten married. While AD could not independently confirm the purchase, reports say that the stars scored a sizable discount on the property, which was listed with a price tag of $11.8 million (£9 million).

Per the Daily Mail’s reporting, the 5,000-square-foot dwelling sits on a one-acre plot and features four bathrooms and four reception rooms. “My youngest is very excited that Spider-Man is going to be living across the street,” an inhabitant of a neighboring home told the Daily Mail. “I told him, ‘You will have to kick a ball a long way to reach their back garden.’ I doubt they will have a housewarming party.”.

Sources indicate that since 2018, Holland has owned a six-bedroom home in Kingston-upon-Thames in southwest London. He paid $3.35 million (£2.5 million) for the six-bedroom residence, which he extensively renovated from 2020 until 2023, when Zendaya reportedly moved in. The Dune star maintains several properties stateside: a $1.4 million five-bedroom, five-bathroom Mediterranean-style house near Los Angeles; a 5,000-square-foot, ranch-style home in Encino, California, for which she paid $3.97 million; and a $4.9 million three-bedroom condo in Brooklyn’s luxe Quay Tower.

The Hollywood pair is likely to remain tight-lipped about their alleged upcoming property, since privacy has been an matter for them in the past. Last year, it was reported that they were spending $1,300 a day on security for their Kingston-upon-Thames dwelling after fans started gathering at the front gates.

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (663 w)

Tech Report: Bitdeer Sells All 281 Bitcoin It Mined Last Week, Holds None

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitdeer sold every bitcoin it mined last week and still holds none of its own, the company mentioned in its latest weekly patch, continuing a nearly year-long strategy of turning production into cash after a weekend plunge in the bitcoin price.
  • According to recent reports, the Singapore-based miner reported output of 281.1 BTC and sales of 281.1 BTC for the week, for a net addition of zero.
  • The sales came as bitcoin fell to a weekend low of $55,106 early Saturday at 1:17 AM ET, Bitcoin Magazine Pro data shows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitdeer sold every bitcoin it mined last week and still holds none of its own, the company mentioned in its latest weekly patch, continuing a nearly year-long strategy of turning production into cash after a weekend plunge in the bitcoin price.

According to recent reports, the Singapore-based miner reported output of 281.1 BTC and sales of 281.1 BTC for the week, for a net addition of zero. Its pure holdings, which exclude customer deposits, were zero as of Nov. 20.

The sales came as bitcoin fell to a weekend low of $55,106 early Saturday at 1:17 AM ET, Bitcoin Magazine Pro data shows. The price has since bounced to near $62,700 as of 11:23 AM ET Monday.

Bitdeer’s treasury shrank from roughly 2,000 BTC at the end of 2025 to zero by Feb. 20, when Bitcoin Magazine reported the miner had liquidated its reserve over eight weeks. At the time, the manufacturer said the move should not be a concern for the broader market.

According to recent reports, bitdeer’s filings show how little it has kept since. In its third-quarter results, filed with the SEC on a Form 6-K on Nov. 10, the firm listed 47 BTC held at Sept. 30, down from 2,029 a year earlier.

It has been revealed that its September production update showed 61 BTC held at the end of August. The tech giant mined 1,355 BTC in September and 3,855 BTC in the third quarter, compared with 1,109 BTC in the same quarter of 2025.

Bitdeer has grown its fleet swiftly. Self-mining hashrate reached 82.3 exahashes per second in the third quarter, up from 35.0 a year earlier, with another 28.7 exahashes per second of co-mining at third-party sites, the quarterly report shows.

Sources indicate that the economics are tight. Self-mining generated $217.5 million in revenue in the quarter but only $6.2 million in gross profit. Electricity averaged $47 per megawatt-hour, and the fleet ran at 15.4 joules per terahash.

Sources indicate that bitdeer posted record revenue of $320.7 million and adjusted EBITDA of $69.6 million, but a net loss of $125.5 million. That included a $54.6 million non-cash loss tied to a bitcoin-collateralized loan from a related party.

Bitdeer also reported $213.7 million in cash and restricted cash, and its board authorized a fresh $100 million share repurchase program on Oct. 8.

Not every miner is selling. American Bitcoin secured a $150 million revolving credit line from FalconX on Monday that is backed by its bitcoin. The tech giant said the facility lets it raise cash without drawing down its reserve.

The loan carries a 5.95% fee and an initial collateral ratio of 143%. Fully drawing it would require about $214.5 million in pledged bitcoin. American Bitcoin has not said whether it has drawn on the line, and its release lists the risk that pledged coins could be liquidated if prices fall.

American Bitcoin, which is majority-owned by Hut 8, said on its Nov. 4 earnings call that it held 8,427 BTC at the end of September. The tech giant has also sold part of its production to cover operating costs.

Industry observers note that other miners have gone the other way. MARA sold 13,597 bitcoin earlier this month, as miners facing thin margins turned to their treasuries for cash.

Shares of Bitdeer (BTDR) were trading near $3.44 at 11:23 AM ET, up about 16% from Friday’s close of $2.96. The stock has ranged from $3.26 to $3.71 on the day as a broad market rally lifted bitcoin-linked stocks after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang.

Bitdeer has not noted whether it intends to rebuild a bitcoin position. It said in February that selling was a liquidity measure tied to evaluating powered land acquisitions and scaling its infrastructure.

The manufacturer is also shifting toward AI cloud services, and it reported an AI cloud revenue backlog of about $2.9 billion in its third-quarter release.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $62,700.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The amount sold exceeded the roughly 24,245 ETH it remarked it held afterward, based on a preliminary, unaudited estimate.
  • According to recent reports, the sell-off also prompted BTCS’s decentralized finance business, Imperium, to pull its capital out of liquidity pools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BTCS sold about 27,300 Ethereum (ETH) on Nov. 20 and used the proceeds to repay $43.8 million of debt on Aave, a decentralized lending protocol, the tech giant disclosed on Nov. 23.

The amount sold exceeded the roughly 24,245 ETH it remarked it held afterward, based on a preliminary, unaudited estimate.

According to recent reports, the sell-off also prompted BTCS’s decentralized finance business, Imperium, to pull its capital out of liquidity pools. That put fees on the withdrawn capital on hold at a business that accounted for most of the tech giant’s third-quarter revenue.

The two decisions were linked by how BTCS financed Imperium. A day before the sale, the organization reported about $54 million in Aave debt, and it borrowed stablecoins against some of its Ethereum and used the proceeds primarily to fund Imperium’s liquidity pool positions.

According to recent reports, BTCS mentioned it monitors the position and can adjust its borrowing as the value of its ETH collateral changes. A drop in the value of pledged ETH can put that collateral at risk of liquidation.

BTCS Chief Executive Charles Allen stated management chose to sell Ethereum and repay Aave to reduce that risk and preserve the company’s ability to meet its obligations on senior secured convertible notes.

“Selling at these prices came at a real cost to the Manufacturer and its shareholders.”.

BTCS borrowed against ether to fund Imperium’s liquidity pools. The November sell-off prompted a debt repayment and a separate pool withdrawal.

Aave debt fell to about $10.5 million after the repayment, while withdrawn capital stopped earning Imperium pool fees.

Debt balances are approximate point-in-time figures. The post-sale estimate is preliminary and unaudited. The separately reported $43.8 million repayment is not calculated by subtracting those rounded balances. Fees refer only to withdrawn capital.

The flow indicates the primary use of the stablecoins, not a dollar allocation. Debt bars start at zero and share a linear scale. The post-repayment bar is drawn at 10.5 ÷ 54 of the November 19 bar length.

Debt balances are approximate point-in-time figures. The post-sale estimate is preliminary and unaudited. The separately reported $43.8 million repayment is not calculated by subtracting those rounded balances. Fees refer only to withdrawn capital.

BTCS reported that about $10.5 million remained on Aave after the repayment, at a loan-to-value ratio of roughly 32%, which measures the outstanding loan against the value of its collateral.

In the same preliminary, unaudited update, BTCS reported aggregate principal on its convertible notes of about $17.9 million, with maturities in May and July 2027.

Recent findings suggest that BTCS’s Nov. 12 earnings release showed that the division generated $3.5 million in third-quarter revenue, about 86% of BTCS’s $4.1 million total.

The firm reported $40.9 million in liquidity pool positions at the end of September, up from $7.6 million at the end of June as Imperium expanded its strategy across Ethereum and Base.

The company notes Imperium earns no pool fees on that capital while it sits outside the pools. Management still prepares to focus the business on Imperium and intends to put the capital back to work when it judges conditions have improved. It gave no date for doing so.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin futures open interest fell 12% last week to $29.3 billion, its lowest level since early March, according to Glassnode's Nov.
  • Industry observers note that over the same week to Nov.
  • It has been revealed that DWF Labs' coin-denominated data showed open interest falling from 712,800 BTC on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin futures open interest fell 12% last week to $29.3 billion, its lowest level since early March, according to Glassnode's Nov. 23 Market Pulse.

Industry observers note that over the same week to Nov. 22, the ratio of short-term-holder supply to long-term-holder supply rose from 15% to 15.5%, its highest since late February. Leveraged traders have thinned out, while recent buyers hold a larger share of the coins, leaving it unclear whether forced selling has ended or shifted to spot holders.

It has been revealed that DWF Labs' coin-denominated data showed open interest falling from 712,800 BTC on Nov. 13 to about 639,900 BTC, a 10.2% decline over a slightly different window, which points to genuine position reduction.

Long-side funding payments fell 53.6% to $803,900, so traders pay roughly half as much to hold bullish perpetual positions. Perpetual cumulative volume delta (CVD) moved from negative $1.5 billion to negative $486.5 million, and spot CVD from negative $170.8 million to negative $120.9 million.

Both readings stayed negative, which describes slower net selling.

According to recent reports, US dollar value of outstanding futures positions at the two weekly readings in Glassnode's Nov. 23 report. The decline reflects both Bitcoin's price and changes in outstanding contracts.

Source: Glassnode — BTC Market Pulse, Nov. 23.

DWF Labs counted over $4.9 billion in crypto-wide liquidations in the week to Nov. 22, including $3.75 billion in longs, about 76%.

The prior week brought nearly $5.8 billion, so roughly $10.7 billion cleared in two weeks. Fewer leveraged positions mean a falling price has less collateral to wipe out. Options traders continue to pay up for protection, as the 25-delta skew rose to 17.4% from 14.4%, its highest since mid-July.

Glassnode's ratio compares short-term-holder supply with long-term-holder supply, a different measure from short-term holders' share of all coins.

The firm classifies entities by average coin age, with a smoothed transition around 155 days, so the ratio can rise as long-term supply falls, as short-term supply grows, or both. A 0.5-point rise is modest, but it arrived while prices fell and futures positions shrank.

Profitable supply fell 6.9%. Both readings come from Glassnode's Nov. 23 report and are rounded to one decimal place.

Source: Glassnode — BTC Market Pulse, Nov. 23.

Supply in profit dropped from 54.2% to 47.3%, leaving 52.7% of circulating supply at a loss or near breakeven.

Short-term-holder net unrealized profit and loss sits at negative 18.3%, its lowest since mid-June. Realized capitalization contracted 0.93% over the month, against 0.06% a week earlier, its weakest reading since July.

US spot Bitcoin ETFs lost about $1.7 billion in the week, the heaviest outflow since early July, and Glassnode puts ETF MVRV at 0.97, which places the average ETF holder below estimated cost basis.

It has been revealed that glassnode's Nov. 17 report supplied the $62,000 to $66,000 cluster where many recent buyers entered, the $74,100 short-term-holder cost basis, the $58,500 June low and the $53,700 realized price as key levels.

From a price near $63,000, $74,100 sits 17.6% higher and $53,700 sits 14.8% lower.

If Bitcoin holds the $62,000 to $66,000 cluster while spot CVD turns positive, ETF outflows reverse, and realized capitalization climbs toward zero, the derivatives reset becomes the base for accumulation.

A move toward $74,100 would then test whether recent buyers can reach breakeven and avoid a rush to sell, while futures positions rebuild gradually behind spot buying.

If Bitcoin fails to hold that cluster while ETF outflows continue and realized capitalization keeps contracting, sellers are holders closing losses, and thin futures positioning offers little cushion.

A break below $58,500 would put the $53,700 realized price in view, and both paths are conditional scenarios built on Glassnode's reference levels.

The derivatives half of the reset is complete, while the spot half awaits evidence of buyers large enough to absorb coins that holders sell at a loss.

Breaking: The Kids Are Outside: The Rise of the Adult Children’s ADU

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Diane and Steve Weaver of Castro Valley, California, shipped their son Sam off to college in 2013, they hoped he’d someday find his dream job and a nice home.
  • While in-law suites and granny flats (a nickname for when ADUs house in-laws) have become popular among young, successful homeowners who want their elderly parents nearby, a growing number of Americans are now adding ADUs to their properties to house adult children threatening to move back in and reverse their status as empty nesters.
  • Blame the return of the flock on the home affordability crisis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Diane and Steve Weaver of Castro Valley, California, shipped their son Sam off to college in 2013, they hoped he’d someday find his dream job and a nice home. And while Sam is thriving professionally as a sales rep with his own place, they never expected that his house would be in their backyard. But the nightmarish Bay Area real estate market made a 400-square-foot ADU (accessory dwelling unit) on his parents’ property, complete with a separate entrance and direct street access, seem like the best option for the 32-year-old. “It was becoming difficult for him to afford rent while also saving toward eventually buying a place of his own,” Diane tells AD. “He’s close by, but it really feels like he has his own home.”.

While in-law suites and granny flats (a nickname for when ADUs house in-laws) have become popular among young, successful homeowners who want their elderly parents nearby, a growing number of Americans are now adding ADUs to their properties to house adult children threatening to move back in and reverse their status as empty nesters.

Diane and Steve Weaver on their property’s ADU.

Blame the return of the flock on the home affordability crisis. These days a homebuyer needs an annual income between $110,000 and $113,000—well above the national average income of $64,220 per year—to comfortably afford a median-priced home in the US, which is right now priced at $434,900. While this has led some grown kids to move back into their childhood bedrooms, in cases where acreage allows, families like the Weavers are opting to be neighbors instead of housemates by setting up self-contained living spaces on the same lot as their single-family homes. In California, they’re certainly no outlier. The state has passed legislation specifically encouraging the construction of ADUs to address the housing shortage—which resulted in quadruple the number of ADU permits issued in the Golden State from 2017 to 2022.

Industry observers note that those in the ADU construction game say families like the Weavers make up an increasingly large slice of their business. Jeremy Nova, co-founder of the Colorado-based prefab ADU builder Studio Home, says ADUs for adult children are popular among his clients because the arrangement is mutually beneficial. The kids are afforded some independence and the ability to save money, “while for the parents, it can also be a long-term investment. The same space that houses an adult child today could eventually become a rental or a separate living space for a caregiver.” ADU builders on the opposite coast are seeing the same demand. Justin Olewack, president of Bolt Builders, says that ADUs for adult children are becoming a top request among his clientele in the DC, Virginia, and Maryland areas, where housing costs have risen 61 percent since 2016.

If it cuts costs and results in a sellable amenity down the line, perhaps moving back home isn’t the failure-to-launch scenario it was once seen as.

An ADU by Studio Home, built in the backyard of a Scottsdale, Arizona, family’s property.

According to recent reports, once a family’s adult child moves out of the property’s ADU, especially if it has a kitchen and bathroom, the structure can serve as a rental, providing passive income for retired parents. Tracy Noh, who hired John Brennan of BZBuild Co to build her daughter Eliza Bowen an ADU in Burbank, was thinking long-term with her compound planning. “An in-home apartment would require sharing the space of our 1,000-square-foot main home. And, as someone who works from home, the ADU seemed a better solution,” she states.

Noh and Eliza show off their Burbank ADU.

It has been revealed that the living arrangement has also enabled Noh and her daughter to develop their own life paths. The structure gives her daughter a space in which she can become a young adult, and Noh the opportunity to step back from making the day-to-day household decisions. The former is learning how to manage her own household: planning meals, budgeting expenses, and making time for household chores.

Sources indicate that “That change in dynamic also allows us both to remain much calmer in our interactions with each other,” Noh claims. It’s not just because there’s a separate place for each of them to retreat to; Noh says she has “gained an enormous amount of respect for Eliza and her ability to manage her own home. It’s a fabulous opportunity to begin to build that adult-to-adult relationship with your child.”.

The interior of Tracy Noh’s ADU by BZBuild Co.

Recent findings suggest that while modest ADUs serve single occupants just fine, more sizable ADUs allow a family’s adult children to bring their own kids in tow. Oren Amir, co-founder of SoCal builder GO Home Builders, points out that in his experience, the catalyst for aging parents to build an ADU for their adult children is almost never just the adult child themselves: It’s the grandchild they will be bringing with them. “The call comes a few months before or after a baby arrives,” he claims. The grandparents don’t want to travel to visit their grandkids; they want them living nearby. Rent in Los Angeles is what stops people from saving, and early parenthood is when saving matters most, Amir says. An ADU in a grandparent’s backyard, therefore, lets the adult children stay in the neighborhood, raise the baby near help, and set some money aside for when the time comes to leave the nest for good. “Everyone gets what they need and nobody has to move in,” Amir says of the arrangement.

While the Weaver family ADU is Sam’s for now, it could grow up to be a granny flat someday. “It’s possible that Sam might live in the main house and we could move into the ADU as we age,” says Diane. “It gives us a lot of options for how the space can be used as our family’s needs change.”.

‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’: Inside the Psychedelic 1970s-Inspired Dystopian Sets

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that francis Lawrence, director of The Hunger Games, has a tradition with author Suzanne Collins.
  • Lawrence’s latest adaptation, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (in theaters today), returns to Panem, a postapocalyptic nation where the ruling Capitol controls twelve districts through extreme systemic oppression—most notoriously the titular spectacle in which children are selected by lottery and forced to fight to the death in an arena.
  • District 12’s female tribute Maysilee Donner (McKenna Grace) at the reaping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that francis Lawrence, director of The Hunger Games, has a tradition with author Suzanne Collins. Before bringing a latest installment of her bestselling dystopian saga to the significant screen, the two join forces to envision how the fictional world of Panem will take shape. “I go to New York each time, and we sit in a conference room at Scholastic,” says Lawrence, who has directed five of the franchise’s six films. “We go through the book page by page and beat out what we think the movie is going to look like.”.

Lawrence’s latest adaptation, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (in theaters today), returns to Panem, a postapocalyptic nation where the ruling Capitol controls twelve districts through extreme systemic oppression—most notoriously the titular spectacle in which children are selected by lottery and forced to fight to the death in an arena. Set twenty-four years before the original The Hunger Games (2012) plotline, the prequel follows District 12’s sixteen-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada)—the future mentor (played by Woody Harrelson) to Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson)—as he is selected to fight in the Second Quarter Quell, a particularly sadistic rendition of the Games held every twenty-five years.

District 12’s female tribute Maysilee Donner (McKenna Grace) at the reaping.

It has been revealed that though the dystopia is set in a future North America, the previous prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (2023), drew from the architecture of 1940s and ’50s postwar Berlin to depict evil President Snow’s rise to tyranny. Set forty years later, Sunrise explores Panem at a new stage of its evolution. Designed by returning production designer Uli Hanisch, the film follows Haymitch from his impoverished mining district, which barely evolves throughout the series’s sixty-five year timeline, to the opulent Capitol, whose extravagance is expressed through a 1970s-inflected visual lexicon.

Sources indicate that “I realized the ’70s fall right smack in the middle between that movie and the originals, so we could lean into that,” notes Lawrence. Hanisch and his team incorporated references to Andy Warhol, Studio 54, and the decade’s psychedelic color palette, appropriating its progressive spirit to convey the Capitol’s opulence and authoritarianism—and, particularly in the arena, using the aesthetic as a means of deception. “To turn the ’70s style from something progressive, liberal, young, and open-minded into something evil is a twist,” says Hanisch. “But that is the key to the entire film’s design.”.

Sources indicate that haymitch and Maysilee as allies in the arena. The forest portion was filmed separately near Cologne, Germany.

Sources indicate that the stylistic choice is also a poignant nod to Collins’s original inspiration for the book series. The 1970s marked a transformation in American television: as color TVs became ubiquitous in households across the country, sporting spectacles, variety indicates, and beauty pageants flourished, establishing cultural touchstones that would help shape the contemporary reality programming Collins critiques and satirizes in The Hunger Games. “I was flipping through the channels one night between reality television programs and actual footage of the Iraq War, when the idea came to me,” Collins recalled in a 2018 interview with The Latest York Times. The juxtaposition inspired her to explore just-war theory for young people through an authoritarian dystopia in which mass entertainment is an instrument of political control.

From an abandoned rural steel mill to authoritarian monuments from postwar Berlin, the film draws on politically charged German sites to capture Panem at a pivotal stage in its political and architectural evolution.

Production Designer Uli Hanisch at the District 12 set. “District 12 is the most sentimental set to me because I’d known this site near my hometown my entire life,” Hanisch claims.

To recreate the Appalachian-inspired, deteriorating industrial landscape of District 12 that was shot in Atlanta in the original series, the production utilized a sprawling abandoned steel mill in Duisburg, Germany, Hanisch’s hometown. “I wish we had it in the original movies, because it is an unbelievable space,” Lawrence states of the post-industrial, rural landscape, which also appeared in The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, Hanisch’s first film in the franchise. “Everywhere you look is exactly how I have always imagined District 12.”.

Industry observers note that while District 12 was filmed near Atlanta in the original films, director Francis Lawrence’s fascination with German architecture brought production to Berlin for The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. It was there that he began collaborating with Berlin-based production designer Hanisch, who proposed this steel mill nearby his hometown for the upcoming location. Upon seeing photographs, Lawrence exclaimed, “Are you kidding me? ... Let’s go tomorrow,” and promptly flew out to see it for himself.

The production designer added modest huts at the edge of a nearby quarry to recreate the Seam, home to Haymitch, his girlfriend Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak), and fellow tribute Louella McCoy (Molly McCann), its humble dwellings contrasting the more prosperous merchant district inhabited by fellow tribute Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace).

“Unlike the Capitol, District 12 doesn't evolve stylistically throughout the films. Nobody is investing in it, and everything is gradually deteriorating,” Hanisch explains. The vivid purples and oranges of the Capitol’s ‘70s palette are notably absent, only appearing prominently in propaganda decorating the reaping square, including Hunger Games campaign materials and posters portraying Snow as Panem’s number-one Peacekeeper.

Druscilla in the Capitol before the tribute interviews, which is broadcast to all of Panem.

In the Capitol, however, the architecture takes on a distinctly ‘70s flair. Rooted in the Roman concept of panem et circenses, or “bread and circuses,” from which Panem takes its name, the architecture reinforces the government’s manipulation through spectacle. In the background is Berlin's International Congress Centrum, a colossal, aluminum-clad convention center that opened in 1979, which Lawrence describes as “Cold War-era Berlin showing off in a modern way.” As West Berlin’s most expensive postwar building, the futuristic complex was publicly subsidised to showcase economic prosperity and technological advancement—an evocative backdrop for the Capitol’s own display of authoritarianism.

“It’s a time of peace for the Capitol with no rebel attacks, so Snow's had time to build the city up in a way that is an extravagant show of power,” Lawrence explains. The chariot parade, which introduces the tributes before the Games, similarly unfolds against the historically-charged Berlin Olympiastadion, which was designed by Werner March for the 1936 Olympics under Nazi Germany to project state power and an illusion of timeless permanence.

Industry observers note that the upstairs library in Plutarch’s home, which he inherited from the Heavensbee dynasty. Reflecting the Capitol’s classic style, it contrasts the Plutarch’s modern downstairs salon which features Warhol-inspired portraits, including one of director Lawrence.

Industry observers note that the Capitol's grandeur is also exhibited inside the mansion of Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), a cameraman with historic ties to Panem’s ruling class. “This was one of my favorite sets because of the scope and scale” Lawrence says, noting how its excess reflects the dynasty's immense wealth. Filmed at Berlin's late-1960s modernist Congress Center, the circular residence required twenty-five vans of retro-modern furniture to fill it. The salon, decked in vibrant 1970s furnishings and Warhol-inspired art, showcases Plutarch's modern sensibilities, in stark contrast to the upstairs library inherited from his family. “We wanted to distinguish Plutarch from the dynasty he comes from,” Lawrence explains, reflecting on how the expansive volumes must be a facade of intellectual sophistication.

Recent findings suggest that the set decoration department spent weeks hand-folding and assembling thousands of hollow cardboard books, interspersed with real volumes, including a collection of Edgar Allan Poe’s poetry, which Plutarch references to Haymitch. “We imagined Plutarch might actually be the first Heavensbee to read some of those books,” Hanisch says. “He even says the library is one of the few worthwhile things his ancestors accomplished.”.

In a recent development, the library's custom-built curved bookshelves envelope the characters, symbolising the insularity of Capitol society. “Circles represent both inclusion and exclusion,” Hanisch states. “If you are in the circle, you're in. And if you're not, you're out.” As fans of the franchise will know, Plutarch (originally played by Philip Seymour Hoffman) later reveals himself as a double agent and leader of the underground rebellion against Snow’s regime.

The aspect ratio expands as Haymitch ascends into the eye-shaped arena, emphasizing the landscape’s immersive scale and beauty. While scouting locations, Lawrence drew inspiration from the dramatic landscapes in Terrence Malick’s A Hidden Life. “I had that in my head, only it was a little trippier. The Asturias were perfect,” he recalls. The kaleidoscopic design also inspired the official logo of the 50th Hunger Games, extending the arena’s psychedelic imagery into the Capitol’s propaganda.

The Quarter Quell arena, in particular, embodies the surreal, fantastical ethos of the 1970s that permeates the film, illustrating how the Capitol exploits beauty to disguise its underlying manipulation and brutality. “As I was reading with Suzanne, I stated there was an Alice in Wonderland-like element to it, which made me think of the song ‘White Rabbit,’ which made me think of the late ’60s, early ’70s,” Lawrence recalls. “That kind of broke something open for me.”.

Industry observers note that designed in the shape of an eye, the eight to ten mile arena serves as a metaphor for the Capitol's omnipresent surveillance. A golden Cornucopia forms its pupil; vibrant meadows its iris; and the surrounding mountain ranges its whites. In the book, Haymitch describes the especially lethal arena masquerading as an idyllic landscape as a “poisonous beauty of an arena.”.

Lawrence and Haymitch in the arena. The physical flowers were concentrated in the foreground, while visual effects extended the colorful landscape into the distance.

Seeking to capture as much natural landscape as possible, Hanisch and location manager Klaus große Darrelmann discovered a remote valley in Asturias, Spain, surrounded by the Cantabrian Mountains. Transforming the isolated valley into a psychedelic paradise proved an enormous undertaking.“The arena was our nemesis,” says Hanisch, recalling how the production had to bring extensive resources to the remote terrain. “You can't even imagine how far away it was or how hard it was to get to.” Crews spent weeks individually installing hundreds of thousands of artificial flowers throughout the meadows and forests.

In a recent development, despite the arena’s dreamlike beauty, water sources, flowers, and vegetation conceal deadly poisons. “It’s the most colorful and playful dystopia you’ll ever see,” producer Nina Jacobson says. Perhaps more than anywhere else in Panem, the arena encapsulates how the Capitol weaponizes the electric zeitgeist of the ‘70s as an instrument of control. “To have something so overwhelmingly beautiful and seductive but poisonous and deadly is very cruel,” Hanisch says. “That contradiction captures the mentality of Panem at this point in its history.”.

Bitcoin developers propose fix for transaction verification gap affecting Lightning wallets

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cryptoslate

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin developers have proposed a new verification system that would allow lightweight wallets to independently authenticate transaction signatures recorded on the blockchain.
  • The draft Bitcoin Improvement Proposal, submitted by developer Jean Pablo on Nov.
  • The proposal could particularly benefit wallets such as Electrum, which supports Bitcoin's Lightning Network and relies on external servers for some blockchain information.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin developers have proposed a new verification system that would allow lightweight wallets to independently authenticate transaction signatures recorded on the blockchain.

The draft Bitcoin Improvement Proposal, submitted by developer Jean Pablo on Nov. 22, addresses a limitation in how wallets verify transaction information received from external servers.

The proposal could particularly benefit wallets such as Electrum, which supports Bitcoin's Lightning Network and relies on external servers for some blockchain information.

Currently, lightweight wallets can verify that a transaction was included in a Bitcoin block using a cryptographic proof tied to its transaction ID, or txid.

However, that identifier excludes witness data, which contains signatures and other information used to authorize spending under Bitcoin's Segregated Witness (SegWit) system.

Consequently, a wallet could successfully verify a transaction's inclusion while holding witness data that differs from what miners actually included in the block.

Pablo's proposal addresses this discrepancy by introducing standardized witness transaction inclusion proofs built around a second identifier, known as the witness transaction ID, or wtxid.

Unlike the conventional transaction ID, the wtxid incorporates witness data, allowing wallets to verify that the full transaction they received matches the version included in a mined block.

The proposed system connects that identifier to Bitcoin's existing witness commitment, which is recorded in the block's coinbase transaction. A second cryptographic proof then connects the coinbase transaction to the block header.

An ordinary proof checks the transaction ID. The draft adds a path from the witness data to the same block header.

A wallet can compare the witness data it received with what a valid block committed to.

Industry observers note that the proposed path assumes a valid block with a SegWit witness commitment. Chain selection and confirmation depth are separate from inclusion verification.

The diagram follows the two proof paths described in the draft and the wallet verification flow in the Bitcoin Core discussion.

Sources indicate that the proposed path assumes a valid block with a SegWit witness commitment. Chain selection and confirmation depth are separate from inclusion verification.

Together, these checks allow wallets to authenticate witness data without downloading and examining the entire block.

The development follows an earlier request from Electrum contributor SomberNight, who sought witness inclusion proofs to strengthen transaction verification for the wallet's Lightning Network functionality.

Lightning wallets interact with Bitcoin's underlying blockchain when opening, closing and monitoring payment channels, making reliable transaction information particularly notable.

The proposed verification system would allow such wallets to independently confirm the witness data supplied by servers while continuing to operate without storing complete blockchain data.

The request previously prompted work on Bitcoin Core, where developers explored extending existing transaction proof commands to cover witness information.

That pull request closed in May without being merged, and developer Sjors Provoost later continued the effort through a separate implementation that introduced commands to generate and verify witness proofs.

Meanwhile, Bitcoin Knots introduced experimental witness-proof support in version 29.1, and Electrum developers have been working on related protocol changes.

However, these efforts use different proof formats, creating compatibility challenges between wallets and the servers providing blockchain information.

Pablo's proposal attempts to resolve those differences by specifying two binary formats and a JSON representation for exchanging and verifying proofs.

The first format provides a separate cryptographic proof for each transaction, while the second reduces duplicated information when verifying multiple transactions together.

In one example involving 10 transactions, the second format reduced proof data from 4,523 bytes to 3,325 bytes, approximately a 26% reduction.

The proposal also includes a Python reference implementation and 93 test cases designed to establish consistent verification behavior across software implementations.

Of those tests, 31 cover proofs that should be accepted, while 62 cover invalid proofs that verification software must reject.

The specification would give Bitcoin Core, Electrum and other wallet developers a common framework for implementing witness verification.

Pablo has requested feedback on the proposed formats and verification requirements, leaving developers to determine whether a shared standard can replace the experimental approaches already in use.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The bitcoin price slipped back to near $61,100 on Monday afternoon, giving up nearly all of its morning spike even as Wall Street held one of its biggest rallies in years on Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.
  • Recent findings suggest that bitcoin jumped above $64,000 shortly after the Nvidia news broke before 10 a.m.
  • According to recent reports, the round trip was costly for leveraged traders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The bitcoin price slipped back to near $61,100 on Monday afternoon, giving up nearly all of its morning spike even as Wall Street held one of its biggest rallies in years on Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin jumped above $64,000 shortly after the Nvidia news broke before 10 a.m. ET and topped out near $64,500. The move reversed within hours, and the bitcoin price dipped to around $60,800 by 2:45 p.m. ET. It remains up only modestly on the day.

According to recent reports, the round trip was costly for leveraged traders. Bitcoin liquidations reached about $321 million, with short bets making up $224 million of that total. Liquidations across the broader crypto market topped $762 million.

Sources indicate that stocks kept climbing while bitcoin slid. The Nasdaq Composite was up about 6.9% near 24,170 at about 3:40 p.m. ET, while the S&P 500 gained about 5% and the Dow rose about 3.2%. The S&P 500 had fallen seven straight days before Monday.

Sources indicate that nvidia (NVDA) led the move, trading near $165.66, up about 32% from Friday’s close of $125.53. The board voted unanimously to bring Huang back as president, CEO and director, 12 days after he resigned.

In a recent development, A stronger dollar may be weighing on the bitcoin price. The dollar index rose about 0.65% to 104.40, its strongest level since April 2025, as the stock rebound put more Federal Reserve rate hikes back in play. The Fed meets Dec. 8-9, and a quarter-point hike remains the base case.

Sources indicate that adam Haeems, head of asset management at Tesseract Group, pointed to steady selling during U.S. market hours since Huang first stepped down. “Bitcoin has fallen in seven of the eight U.S. sessions since Huang went, today’s included, and last week each session’s fall lined up with that day’s ETF outflow,” he mentioned.

Crypto stocks held up far better than the bitcoin price. Strategy (MSTR) was up about 9.3% near $85.03 in afternoon trading, after it disclosed a purchase of 457 bitcoin last week. Coinbase (COIN) gained about 6.7% to near $108.78, Robinhood (HOOD) rose about 8.8% to near $67.64 and Circle (CRCL) added about 8% to near $51.33.

Industry observers note that miners with AI data center businesses posted the biggest moves. IREN (IREN) jumped about 23% to near $14.57, CleanSpark (CLSK) rose about 12.6% and MARA Holdings (MARA) gained about 10%. Core Scientific (CORZ) climbed about 9.4% and Riot Platforms (RIOT) added about 7.1%.

According to recent reports, monday’s spot bitcoin ETF flows are the next test. The funds lost about $1.79 billion last week, their fourth straight week of net outflows, as bitcoin slid toward $58,000 on Friday and hit a weekend low near $55,100.

Recent findings suggest that “Tonight’s ETF flow figure is the first real test of this bounce,” Haeems said. Strong inflows would suggest buyers are returning, while another round of outflows would raise doubts about how far the rebound can run.

Sources indicate that traders also face Wednesday’s inflation data and thin trading around Thanksgiving in a holiday-shortened week. Wintermute OTC trader Jasper De Maere stated he isn’t ready to call a bottom for the bitcoin price. “A few days of data do not confirm a trend and these series turn slowly,” he said.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $61,100.

The 7-inch inseam hits the sweet spot—enough coverage for confidence, but still letting your legs breathe.

It’s that happy blend of 86 percent polyester and 14 percent elastane, softly swishy and sweat-wicking to keep you cool, even if the guy next to you in spin class is not.

Sources indicate that sizing is true to fit, with inseams ranging from 5 inches for size small to 7 inches for 2XL. At $68, they’re not the cheapest, but they’re versatile enough to justify it. Throw on a hoodie, and you’re smoothie-bar ready. Functional, stylish, and just flashy enough to make you the coolest guy in the gym—just don’t get caught doing arm curls in the squat rack.

Skip the cotton—it’s a sweat sponge. Synthetic fabrics like polyester blends are moisture-wicking and dry quickly, while nylon blends are more breathable for hot weather. Look for spandex or elastane for that four-way stretch, so you can move freely without restriction. Bonus: Some materials, like merino wool, are naturally anti-stink, while others feature built-in odor-fighting technology to keep you smelling fresh, no matter how hard you go.

Lined shorts offer built-in support, making them ideal for high-impact activities. "Unlined shorts offer more versatility for layering, while lined shorts provide additional support and comfort for high-impact activities," says Hamlin. If you’re lifting heavy or going ape on the air bike, the liner is a win. For casual workouts or layering over tights, unlined shorts let you move freely and stay cool.

Recent findings suggest that the inseam is the length of the shorts from your nether region to the inside hem, and getting it right can make or break your workout. If you’re doing moves like squats, lunges, or anything that’s got you moving deep and low, shorter inseams (think 5 to 7 inches) are your best bet for keeping things smooth and unrestricted. While shorter inseams offer better mobility, longer inseams of 9 to 11 inches are great for taller athletes or anyone who wants extra coverage. Just keep in mind, if you’re on the shorter side, too much fabric can feel bulky and might even slow you down.

Sources indicate that functional storage is a must. "I say pockets are a must for me, and an extra bonus if they zip. Not a pocket in the back of my waist that I can barely reach, but pockets on the front sides," states Andy Stern from Rumble Boxing. Side pockets keep your essentials handy, and zippers keep you from chasing keys mid-jog.

Your gym shorts should feel as good as they look. Elastic waistbands with drawstrings keep you secure, while lightweight, breathable fabrics keep you comfortable and focused. Gym shorts should fit snugly around your waist—no squeezing, no sliding down mid-squat. Think "secure but free to move," like your gym buddy who knows when to spot you and when to back off. If you’re lunging and your shorts are riding up, it’s time to re-evaluate.

Sources indicate that when it comes to picking gym shorts, it’s all about matching your moves. If you’re running, go for shorter inseams and split hems—you want freedom of movement, not fabric flapping around like you’re in a wind tunnel. Plus, reflective details keep you visible, because dodging traffic shouldn’t be part of your cardio. For lifting, you’ll need durable fabrics and compression liners to keep everything secure while you chase your personal best—nobody needs a wardrobe malfunction mid-squat. And for yoga? Think soft, stretchy, and unlined, so you can nail that downward dog without feeling like your shorts are plotting against you.

According to recent reports, flattering shorts come down to fit, proportion, and the right inseam for your build. If you’ve got beefy legs, short shorts will always work in your favor. Show them off with a 5-inch inseam (or less), which hits mid-thigh for most guys. For a touch more coverage, go with a 7-inch inseam, the most popular length for a casual, everyday look. Aim for a slight taper through the leg so it holds its shape without clinging. Bonus points for a smooth waistband that won’t dig in.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, it’s my job to try and test all kinds of gym shorts. I also enlisted help from our team of style and fitness editors, including members of our Men's Health advisory board. For months, we personally tested dozens of workout shorts. These weren’t casual try-ons; we put them through their paces in real training sessions.

Sources indicate that our evaluation focused on four key areas: comfort, performance (think moisture-wicking, quick-drying, and breathability), type (lined or unlined), and durability. Comfort and functionality are non-negotiable, especially for guys tackling intense training. Our mission? To find gym shorts that not only look great but also withstand tough workouts and the test of time.

Industry observers note that we weren’t interested in trendy or fad-driven designs. Instead, we prioritized gym shorts that work for athletic guys who train hard, offer exceptional value at reasonable price points, and maintain a timeless style. The result? A curated list of six gym shorts that feel great, perform even better, and will look sharp for years to come.

#167347. Tech Report: Cycling Taught Me How to Suffer—a Lesson That Helped Me Lose 140 Pounds and Find Recovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1785 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Menshealth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Cycling Taught Me How to Suffer—a Lesson That Helped Me Lose 140 Pounds and Find Recovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1785 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that SEPTEMBER 2026, THE week of the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal and the city was lousy with bicycles.
  • Sources indicate that I'd heard elite cyclists—guys like Toms Skujins, Sean Quinn, and Mike Woods—talk about this pain in passing, but I was in Montreal to learn more.
  • IN 2001, I was an obese drug addict.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that SEPTEMBER 2026, THE week of the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal and the city was lousy with bicycles. On most corners, a new pack of amateur cyclists gathered. Bixi—Montreal’s bike share program—was represented, but as a garnish to the inundation of mountain, beach, fixie, and road bikes, along with their riders from around the world, taking over the city. I watched all this in awe. Cycling changed me because it taught me how to suffer. The sport familiarized me with the type of suffering that wrecks you, but you put yourself through it on purpose. You suffer to emerge resilient and better.

Sources indicate that I'd heard elite cyclists—guys like Toms Skujins, Sean Quinn, and Mike Woods—talk about this pain in passing, but I was in Montreal to learn more. I wanted to know if they saw the power of suffering in the same way I did.

IN 2001, I was an obese drug addict. Checking into rehab that year put a number to my weight: 536 pounds. I’d been diagnosed with congestive heart failure, drugs were promptly killing me, and I was motivated to change. Once I’d been sober for a year, I was able to see that my weight was causing me suffering.

Standing was a herculean effort, placing my feet in the right spot to support me, calculating the angle my knees would be in at the apex of my shifting mass, deep breath, locked core, and a hope and a prayer that I didn’t topple. Tying my shoes was done in bursts of held breath and near-blackouts. I slept sitting up, because the pressure of my chest caused me to choke and gasp. I could once soothe that suffering with food and drugs and kick that discomfort down the road a bit, but in sobriety I needed healthy outlets.

Recent findings suggest that I’d successfully managed lose 100 pounds before my wife tricked me into going to the gym. When she’d ask that I go, I’d tell her that the gym was a place for fit people. So she bought me a package with a personal trainer, said I could flake on the appointments, but I’d be flushing money down the toilet if I did. I went, but I was geared towards avoidance, and whenever something in the gym got hard, I’d just tell the trainer I couldn’t do it.

In a recent development, riding a bike was something I did during outings with my wife and little kids maybe a few times a year. We’d cram our minivan full of bikes, find the flattest part of the Venice bike path, and slowly cruise for ten minutes at a time. Getting them back into the car was the hardest thing I had to work through.

Little did I know that someday cycling would be the key to changing my life.

ROUND AND ROUND I went losing and regaining weight. In 2009, after getting down to 300 pounds and ballooning back up to over 400, faced with having to start over once again, I turned my sights to running.

In a recent development, I tried running on a desolate stretch of the LA river near my house in Studio City. Not only was I unbearably slow, running hurt. My flat feet sent electric jolts of white-hot pain cascading up and through my body. That first day, I’d wrapped my ankles so tightly with ace bandages that my toes went numb. My feet were no better off and my nipples bled. The next day I could barely stand. The suffering didn’t stop when I stopped running. My feet, ankles, knees, and hips hurt long after—and I had no control over it.

Sources indicate that with running out, but I turned to an old beach cruiser in our shed. The street we lived on was relatively flat, but every street branching off it was a steep climb. After a few rounds on my street, I decided to be ballsy and see how long I could last going uphill.

It has been revealed that my legs were screaming, but there was no electric jolt of pain in my pedal stroke. My heart thundered, my mind told me I had to stop. But without the jarring jolt I got when my feet hit the ground while running, I knew I could go further.

Industry observers note that despite never riding my bike uphill as a kid, despite weighing 400 pounds, despite every physical and mental signal in me telling me to quit, I made it up to the top of that hill, up to Mulholland and Laurel Canyon, and it was glorious. Fighting through that urge to stop was incredible; getting to the top even more so. The pain while running was a warning that stayed with me after I stopped. The pain of cycling uphill was legs, lungs, and heart. I could push through it, and it stopped when I stopped.

I asked Tour de France cyclist Mike Woods about this distinction of suffering when I was in Montreal. “Suffering is a bit of a misnomer for endurance events. Are you really suffering? It’s elected, you know?” he told me. “You choose the pain, you choose when to stop, you choose when to keep going. I don’t truly suffer. Suffering is when you don’t choose for that pain to be inflicted on you”.

And then he said something that really resonated with me: “But it does prepare you for real suffering, when you have something bad happen to you in life. Doing endurance events, I find—it’s fake suffering, but when you have those bad moments in your life, you’re better prepared to manage them.”.

It has been revealed that AFTER THAT HILL climb, I started riding my bike regularly, eventually graduated to a mountain bike, and then to a road bike. I rode to the top of every mountain in Los Angeles. I discovered I was capable of so much more than my mind or body allowed me to believe. Legs screaming, heart pounding, mind numbing, this was suffering, and I found that I loved it. And, like Woods said, I found that the more I suffered on a bicycle, the less I suffered off it.

Recent findings suggest that “One day at a time, one pedal stroke at a time. Just move forward,” Toms Skujins, a two-time Latvian road race champion, told me in Montreal. “When you’re racing, you can stop at any point. You’re the one doing the damage, you know? That’s very voluntary suffering, because there’s, obviously, things in the world that happen where you don’t choose to suffer, and you have no choice there. Here… if your legs are screaming too much, you can just stop. For me, that kind of suffering is definitely easier to take.”.

Industry observers note that within my first year of cycling, I was riding every day. There was a loop that took me from Studio City over the hill to West Hollywood. I’d cross Los Angeles, ride up PCH, cross the Santa Monica Mountains, and ride back to Studio City along Ventura Boulevard. It got me 100 miles and 8,000 feet of climbing, and I did it a few times a week. I’d do shorter 30- to 50-mile rides on the remaining days.

In a recent development, sean Quinn, a US pro cyclist, gets it: “It sounds easy when you’re sitting on the couch, but when you’re actually in that moment suffering, your body’s basically sending you all the signals it can to make you just do anything else, just stop, stop the suffering,” he told me. “There’s no instant fix to a lot of your suffering. You have to be patient, accept that it’s gonna be shitty for a while, and wait it out, and keep a cool head, and eventually it does get better. Of course, you have to take action.”.

Sources indicate that when I was riding every day, I got down to 213 pounds. I’d like to say I stayed there. But I went back to work, stopped riding, my diet unraveled, and over the next few years, I gained nearly all of it back.

In 2016, 400 pounds again, I ruptured the biceps tendon in my right arm and had to have surgery to repair it. As a sober guy, I turned down the post-op painkillers. I was up all night in pain and had to work the following day. On set, with the motion of production buzzing around me, the pain was dull, but it was unrelenting, just like a ride up Angeles Crest Highway, more than 120 miles out-and-back, with over 13,000 feet of elevation gain. I hadn’t chosen the injury, but I had chosen to go without the pills, and that reminded me of the pain on the bike, something I picked and something I knew would come to an end. I’d remind myself of that and go back to learning my lines and preparing for the scene.

That day reminded me that I knew how to do this. So I got back on a diet, and by 2018 I was down to 260, and I’ve held steady there ever since.

According to recent reports, riding a bike taught me that I could suffer now in benefit of tomorrow. It’s been the most powerful lesson I’ve learned about myself.

ON THE DAY of the elite men’s road race, we fans lined the streets. There was dedicated bike parking near the finish line—Fans Village Bonjour Montreal—with thousands of bikes in neat rows. We all lined up to watch the attacks, riders going solo for that long and treacherous circuit. An American, Brandon McNulty, went off the front with about three laps to go and won the World Championship this year. It was thrilling to see. At the press conference afterward he said, “I was just dying, but I kept pushing.”.

Leaving Canada, I couldn’t help but think that I shared something with everyone else there for the races. A secret membership, dues paid in sweat, and a code, to respect and revel in my voluntary suffering.

I’d gone to Montreal to ask the riders if they saw suffering the way I did, and in different words, all three told me that what you do on the bike carries over into the rest of your life. I’d thought cycling taught me how to suffer, but what it did was give me a place where I was in control of it, where I could make it a practice, so that when the suffering of life came along, the suffering I had no control over, I was better equipped to deal with it.

In the Berkshires, an Intensely Yellow Kitchen Is Anything but Mellow in This Lakeside Cottage

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1407 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that “I personally would not want this yellow in my kitchen,” notes Jess Cooney.
  • In a recent development, cooney’s clients didn’t blink at the bold idea.
  • Industry observers note that cooney’s clients weren’t initially convinced by reclaimed brick flooring in the entryway, but Cooney’s team proved convincing—they believed the space needed a worn palette to counterbalance the intensely yellow kitchen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that “I personally would not want this yellow in my kitchen,” notes Jess Cooney. It’s a cheeky comment about the beaming hue she herself chose for clients in the Berkshires—a color that defines their entire lakeside home, one she calls the diva of the whole project, requiring (no, demanding) decisions in every square foot to balance out its intensity.

In a recent development, cooney’s clients didn’t blink at the bold idea. Unusually carefree for a couple with high-powered jobs, they gave the AD PRO Directory designer free license to create. The bungalow was purchased as a weekend retreat from life in Newly introduced York, but even before paint swatches were discussed, the kitchen was a sticking point. “The kitchen was crazy—it was this tiny little makeshift kitchen,” says Cooney.

Industry observers note that cooney’s clients weren’t initially convinced by reclaimed brick flooring in the entryway, but Cooney’s team proved convincing—they believed the space needed a worn palette to counterbalance the intensely yellow kitchen. Much to their clients’ delight, it worked beautifully. A Croft House Morro Credenza with leather-front doors anchors the space, topped with a vintage lamp from Millerton Antiques Center and set beneath an unknown artwork from Brimfield Flea Market.

Cooney opted to stain wood-paneled walls in custom blue and brown stains from Rubio Monocoat, allowing rustic grains to shine through. Atop a Jaipur Hazan rug, an upholstered George Smith Emma Ottoman anchors the room and is accompanied by a set of armchairs and a velvet mordoré sofa from Lawson-Fenning. A 20th-century oil painting by Paul Berg hangs above the reworked fireplace, while in the corner, above a Charles Dudouyt side table, hangs a vintage painting sourced from The Little Store in Massachusetts.

It has been revealed that “We just decided to kind of lean into it and go almost in a maximalist way,” states Cooney of the dining room’s focal point, a painting by K.G. Narendra Babu that inspired the home’s many colors. For the inside of a Four Hands Camila Sideboard, they commissioned artisan Joel Haynes to hand-paint a leafy pattern. A Hubbardton Forge Disq fixture hangs above a custom Bossi dining table surrounded with Tribute Modern Dining Chairs from Craft Associates.

The husband, an English lawyer, craved a small cabin in the woods, while the wife, an Italian who loves cooking, wanted a home large enough to host intimate gatherings. “This house was a happy compromise,” states the husband. But while the home spans three levels and around 4,500 square feet, the main floor measured just about 1,000. The kitchen, in a cramped corner, didn’t cut it.

Industry observers note that cooney’s team reconfigured a few walls. They collapsed oversized closets in the entryway, shrinking the space to a slimmer mudroom while letting the entire layout exhale, expanding the footprint of the semi-open cooking area. The room is now the proper heart of the home, and its bright yellow cabinets aren’t shy about it.

Cabinets with glass windows were fabricated by Westek Architectural Woodworking and feature an array of white porcelain that punctuates and calms the intensely painted millwork; the pieces were all sourced from shops in the Berkshires, including Millerton Antiques, All that Jazz, and Montage Antiques.

“It’s the diva of the project,” claims Cooney of the yellow Benjamin Moore paint used throughout the kitchen, a choice that influenced nearly all palettes throughout the home. Ceilings, walls, and upper cabinets were painted in Farrow & Ball’s Fresh White.

It has been revealed that the kitchen island is topped with a wooden counter and is paired with Amber Interiors Cade Counter Stools in walnut. A set of Matthew Fairbank Allegro Pendants hang above the island.

In a recent development, the saturated hue, Benjamin Moore’s Glen Ridge Gold, wasn’t a choice made on a whim. Like many colors peppering the home, it was inspired by a painting by Chennai-based artist K.G. Narendra Babu that now hangs in the couple’s dining room. The artwork was given to the couple by a family member who worked in India, and it features an array of folk and musical motifs.

“The whole point of the project is that it’s bright and energetic and deeply relaxing at the same time,” claims Cooney. “That was the trust that they put in us—to believe that both could happen.”.

The architecture itself lacked a definitive style. Light traces of Arts & Crafts style gave Cooney a point of view to reinvent existing character. A fireplace in the living room is now reimagined with glazed brick Clé tiles, their dappled surface cladding the surround with clean lines and a crafted look; a custom stain allowed wood-paneled walls to bear rustic grains but in modern blue-green tones.

Recent findings suggest that to expand the kitchen’s footprint, Cooney reclaimed space from unnecessarily large closets in the entryway. Her team moved the wall to install smaller, but equally useful, cabinets that turn the space into a mudroom. The custom millwork, crafted by Westek Architectural Woodworking and painted in Farrow & Ball’s Blue Gray, complements a vintage rug and a built-in bench.

In a recent development, A custom walnut vanity injects warmth as an alternative to a colder stone. Cooney’s team used a boat sealer to coat and protect the walnut, giving the material a high-gloss finish. A fabric shade made with Eric Kuster’s Micha 002 textile occupies the space that might traditionally feature a mirror. “You can kind of break a rule and have it be playful and fun, especially in a powder bath,” claims Cooney, noting that a mirror hangs on the side wall instead. The wallcovering is Pierre Frey’s Uberon print.

In a recent development, cooney describes an almost cottagey feel in the primary, thanks to a walnut Flora Bed by Jacob May, which was locally made and turned by hand, layered with cozy and textural textiles like Parachute Home’s Hand Stitched Cotton Quilt. Gentle patterns add to the mix through a Scandinavian kilim with geometric design from Rug & Kilim, and light drapes made with a Best Buds textile by Kerry Joyce.

Sources indicate that making the most of existing features, light touches to the bathroom reimagined the space, like painting existing wainscoting in Farrow & Ball’s Tanner’s Brown, and covering the walls in a botanical House of Hackney Herbarium wallpaper. For a touch of texture, Cooney also layered vintage rugs and set an antique Victorian bamboo chair in the corner below the window.

Recent findings suggest that with a view over the living room, Cooney states the lofted floor is like a little escape within the small cottage. Leaning into the cozy feel, the team went with a layered look. A brass chest anchors the space, paired with a black armchair owned by the clients, which was reupholstered with a burgundy fabric from Abraham Moon & Sons, and a Lawson-Fenning Morro Sectional in a linen blend.

Recent findings suggest that the clients’ only real hesitation was a bit of a surprise: the reclaimed brick Cooney specified for the mudroom. It is laid in a herringbone pattern with colors that appeared to shift across the surface. That yellow kitchen? Totally fine. But the expressive bricks? Too dramatic. “We relied on the team’s judgement, and this feature is now one of our most favorite parts of the home,” says the husband, noting how guests often compliment the mudroom.

Industry observers note that “I feel like this house is kind of us unchecked,” says Cooney of her clients’ trust. “No one checked us, so we were allowed to do the fullest extent of what we wanted to do.” Her clients could easily have staged their own diva moment after the cabinets were painted in screaming yellow, before everything else around it fell into place around it; but they let the vision come into full focus.

In a recent development, as if cantilevered over the hill, a screened-in porch is the best of both worlds. “You don’t have to have everything be indoor-outdoor in a covered porch—you can really pull the inside out there and not worry so much,” says Cooney, nodding to choices like Henning Kjaernulf dining chairs from the 1960s purchased from Lone Fox. And while most might use a lighter color in this space, Cooney chose a deeper Farrow & Ball Hopper Head paint for the walls and window frames, which she says helps punctuate the view in a beautiful way.

The view overlooking the Berkshires.
